Declarations of Pecuniary Interest under the “Municipal Conflict of Interest Act”
Susan Doyle, CAO, Supportive Housing in the Province (SHIP)
CSD-HOU-26-001, 10 Year Housing and Homelessness Plan Update
notes:
Ryan Pettipiere, Director, Housing Services, introduced the report, noting that the 10 Year Housing and Homelessness Plan is a legislated requirement and that the report outlines the Region's approach to meeting the provincial scope of direction. He explained that the Region's approach to the 10 Year Housing and Homelessness Plan is based on existing planning frameworks that target each section of the housing continuum, and that the completed Plan must be submitted to the Province by the end of May for review and feedback.

In response to the Committee, R. Pettipiere confirmed that the Plan to End Chronic Homelessness sits within the larger umbrella of the 10 Year Housing and Homelessness Plan.

R. Pettipiere also confirmed that as part of the submission of this Plan to the Province, the need for additional funding from upper levels of government will be highlighted. 

R. Pettipiere explained that future changes to data collection methods will improve the ability to desegregate data surrounding housing and homelessness.

R. Pettipiere clarified that the total financial investment needed to resolve homelessness in Waterloo Region will be articulated to the province, including the breakdown of federal, provincial, and municipal investment and how much additional funding is required to meet the housing need. He also noted the need to balance investing in both upstream initiatives and in measures that respond to immediate housing needs. 

Peter Sweeney, Commissioner of Community Services, confirmed that coordination with other municipalities and service system managers takes place to ensure messaging to the Province regarding investment is consistent across municipalities. 

In response to the Committee, R. Pettipiere confirmed that there is some data breakdown of the gender of individuals experiencing homelessness, noting that approximately 65% are male-identifying and approximately 35% are female-identifying. He also noted that the Point in Time Count tries to enumerate hidden homelessness, but acknowledged that homelessness will most likely always be underrepresented due to the difficult nature of quantifying such data.

P. Sweeney clarified that $200 million of Provincial funding allocated to the Region was for use Region-wide, not specifically for housing and homelessness initiatives. He also noted that the ratio of municipal to provincial funding for homelessness programs in the last budget cycle was 1:1.

R. Pettipiere confirmed that the Region does compare its housing and homelessness statistics and initiatives against other municipalities. 

The Committee expressed concerns surrounding hidden homelessness and how this disproportionately affects women.

In response to the Committee, R. Pettipiere explained that the Prioritized Access to Housing Support (PATHS) waitlist program prioritizes highest level of need balanced with chronological order on the waitlist. R. Pettipiere confirmed decisions are managed on a case-by-case basis. 

Received for information.

items.title: CSD-HOU-26-002, Waterloo Region Housing Revitalization – Mooregate Redevelopment
notes:
P. Sweeney, provided opening remarks on the report, reminding Council that in November 2025 staff were directed to return with options related to the Waterloo Region Housing Revitalization Plan by the end of 2026 Q1.

R. Pettipiere noted that staff have worked with cost consultants to model various scenarios that could potentially move the Mooregate redevelopment project forward, but that the consultants concluded that none of the scenarios would be feasible without a significant capital contribution from the Region. He further noted that staff have recommended that the project continue to be postponed while other potential opportunities are explored through the issuance of an expression of interest framework specific to working with not-for-profits and co-ops. 

In response to Committee's concerns for Mooregate's relocated tenants, R. Pettipiere confirmed that all tenants have been relocated, with the majority of tenants being relocated to other Waterloo Region Housing properties. He also confirmed that communication with tenants on the status of Mooregate will continue to take place.

In response to the Committee, R. Pettipiere confirmed ongoing sitework is taking place to prepare the site for future projects. 

P. Sweeney confirmed that this project is a priority and staff are moving as quickly as possible while ensuring appropriate procurement and legal requirements are met.

R. Pettipiere confirmed meetings with Build Canada Homes (BCH) are scheduled, but that at this time nothing formal has been presented to BCH for consideration. 

R. Pettipiere noted that connecting with neighbourhood associations, ward councillors, and previous tenants are next steps for staff.

In response to the Committee, R. Pettipiere confirmed that approximately 11,500 individuals are currently on the Region's centralized waitlist for housing.

items.title: Strategic Priority - Equitable Services and Opportunities
PDL-BWR-26-003, Youth Voices Driving Community Change – CYPT Data in Action
notes:
Matthew Chandy, Director, Build Waterloo Region, introduced the report, noting that the ongoing Data in Action work is a youth-led initiative that is rooted in the 2023 Youth Impact Survey and the data is now being extracted to prioritize areas of focus that have been identified by youth.

Jim Moss, Co-Chair, Children and Youth Planning Table (CYPT), highlighted that data collection lead to six priority actions identified by children and youth.

Adan Imran, Youth Connector, noted that 1,800 young people in Waterloo Region responded to the 2023 Youth Impact Survey and explained that next steps for the CYPT include connecting with leaders in the priority action areas to bridge connections between leaders and youth.

J. Moss noted that the end goal of the three-year Youth Impact Survey cycle is to arrive at priority action area strategies and build these into the CYPT's Strategic Plan. He also noted that the next cycle and data collection phase will begin on May 1.

In response to the Committee, J. Moss noted that children and youth both in Waterloo Region and across the country are experiencing challenges to their mental health, and that to adequately address this, children and youth must be carefully considered in the initiatives that are implemented in the Region.

In response to the Committee, J. Moss clarified that while issues such as mental health and addictions did appear in the initial list of 600 action items identified by youth during the survey process, these issues ranked as less pressing and thus did not appear within the top six priority actions identified. He also noted that today's youth demographics are currently in the upstream, chronologically, of addictions issues in comparison to previous generations.

A. Imran further noted that while mental health is not explicitly mentioned within the six priority actions, the six identified actions often target the root causes of mental health concerns.

J. Moss confirmed that an initial list of 600 action items was distilled down to a list of 40 actions, and then even further distilled into six priority actions. Alison Pearson, Manager, Children and Youth Planning Table, clarified that while the CYPT addresses only the six priority actions, CYPT supports community service providers in addressing other actions from the list of 40.

A. Pearson confirmed that there is overlap between the work of the CYPT and the Community Safety and Wellbeing Plan, and that efforts are being made to collaborate on shared issues and establish connections between the work of the two initiatives. 

In response to the Committee, J. Moss clarified that to be recognized as a centre of excellence on child and youth wellbeing, the CYPT would need to enter into longitudinal studies, which would require additional funding and expertise. He also noted that there is interest from the University of Waterloo in collaborating on this. 

A. Imran also noted that the number of survey respondents could be used to measure the CYPT's impact, highlighting that the first Youth Impact Survey had only 300 responses in comparison to the 2023 Survey, which had 1,800 responses.

J. Moss further noted that without further investment, measuring impact and tracking of change can be difficult, as many of the CYPT's partner organizations do not have the capacity or resources to provide detailed measurements of their own impact. 

A. Imran also expressed that the CYPT provides a space for youth to develop leadership skills and have their voices amplified.

J. Moss encouraged the Committee to communicate directly with youth in response to their priority actions to develop a stronger bridge of trust. 

In response to the Committee, J. Moss noted that previous Youth Impact Surveys lacked representation from certain groups, including Indigenous youth. He explained that data collection methods have evolved since the past survey was administered, and statistically weighted targets for each demographic group have now been established as well as differentiated communication strategies.

In response to the Committee, A. Imran agreed that youth often experience difficulty in securing employment, citing concerns with the culture surrounding employment that expects candidates to be overqualified for positions.

In response to concerns from the Committee regarding bullying in schools, J. Moss noted that the CYPT speaks on behalf of youth at trustee meetings and works to build strong relationships with the school boards, but acknowledged that this is an area in which the CYPT needs to grow.

In response to the Committee, A. Pearson noted that the CYPT places a heavy importance on its accountability to young people and strives to ensure that the results of young people's input and efforts can be demonstrated to them.

J. Moss emphasized the importance of ensuring that young people feel a sense of belonging in Waterloo Region. In response to the Committee, he also spoke about the benefits that restricting the use of social media amongst young people can have.

In response to the Committee, A. Imran emphasized that students should be able to express political opinions and noted that she disagreed with the Minister of Education's direction to avoid expressing political views during graduation ceremonies.

In response to the Committee, J. Moss noted that the CYPT can assist with facilitating interactions and conversations between Councillors and youth.

In response to the Committee, J. Moss clarified that the 600 youth who participated in the information gleaning after survey results were captured may not have been the same youth who participated in the survey. He explained that for privacy reasons, personal contact details are not linked to individual survey results, and therefore survey participants could not be contacted directly to confirm their participation in the information gleaning process.

A. Pearson also noted that surveys may not be the preferred method of providing input for all youth, and often a different group of youth voices are captured in the group discussion process of data analysis after survey results are collected.

A. Imran confirmed that the initial 600 action items were refined in an intergenerational space, but that emphasis was placed on youth voices during this process, with support from adults.

In response to questions from the Committee regarding the 2021 Youth Impact Survey, J. Moss noted that 2021 saw a flare up of acute mental health challenges related to the Covid-19 pandemic.

Received for information.
